name: patch/apply
about: Applying a patch to a client's cache. Every other area in this pack is about what a server produces; this one is about what a client does with it, which is where the protocol's promise about screens staying current is actually kept or broken. A client that applies these differently does not fail loudly - it shows the wrong data.
source: spec 13, which states the rules, and 04 §2/§2b, which define the operations. Each case is an initial result, a patch, and the result a client must hold afterwards, materialised - so the expectation is readable and says nothing about how a cache stores anything.

cases.name: set merges the fields it names and leaves the rest
cases.why: field-level, not a replacement: a patch that named only `stock` must not lose the title

cases.name: set applied twice is set applied once
cases.why: spec 13 §4: a merge of the same fields is the same merge, which is what makes `set` safe to receive twice

cases.name: operations apply in order
cases.why: a patch is a sequence, not a set

cases.name: del removes the row and leaves the others where they were
a del and the list operation for the same removal together remove one row
cases.why: **the case that matters most, and the one that was wrong.** A command's `del` and its live query's positional `list` operation describe one removal and both reach the client that ran the command. `list` positions name the list as the server last sent it, so a client that shortens its list on `del` then applies `del: [0]` to whatever moved into the slot - one removal, two rows gone. A deleted row has to keep its position until the positional operation has been applied.

cases.name: del twice is del once
cases.why: removing what is gone removes nothing

cases.name: list removes the named positions, then inserts at the new ones
cases.why: `del` names positions in the list the client holds; `ins` names positions after those removals. Reading either against the wrong list puts the row in the wrong place

cases.name: an insertion carries the row, so it is stored as well as placed
cases.why: the `set` afterwards reaches it, which it only can if the insertion stored the entity rather than just placing a value in a list

cases.name: a set of a row in the list reaches it wherever the list holds it
cases.why: normalisation is the point: one entity, however many results mention it

cases.name: a field selected under an alias stays with the result, and a set changes only the entity's own fields
cases.why: x is what this result asked for, not a field of the book: kept on the entity it was overwritten by any other result selecting another field as x (spec 07 §3). A set names the book's own fields, so stock follows it and x waits for the result to be read again

cases.name: at merges fields into the plain object at a path of this result
cases.why: spec 13 §2: the path is dotted with array positions included, `""` is the result itself, and the merge names fields rather than replacing the object - `name` stays

cases.name: inv marks an entity stale and keeps what the client holds
cases.why: spec 13 §2: the client refetches on next read; it does not discard what it holds. Only the named entity is marked, and marking an entity is not marking the results that hold it - that is invOp

cases.name: a set clears the staleness an inv left
cases.why: spec 13 §2: a set clears staleness for that entity, so the order matters - the same two operations the other way round leave it stale

cases.name: invOp marks this operation's results stale and keeps what they hold
cases.why: a result marked stale is refetched on next read, and read until then: invOp is not a delete

cases.name: guard: invOp of another operation leaves this result fresh
cases.why: or the case above passes against a client that marks every result stale on any invOp

cases.name: a deleted root entity reads as null
cases.why: spec 13 §5: a result whose root entity was deleted holds null, which is what a nullable query would have answered anyway. Not an empty object, and not a dangling reference

cases.name: a nested entity in set is stored in its own right, not copied into its parent
cases.why: spec 13 §2: nested entities in `value` are themselves stored and replaced by references. The other book reaching the new name is the only way to see that: a cache that kept the author inside Book:b1 shows two authors where there is one

cases.name: a del reaches a list held in another entity's field
cases.why: spec 13 §2: every reference goes, from results and from other entities' fields alike. The list here belongs to Author:a1, not to the result, so a cache that only cleans its results leaves a dangling reference behind

cases.name: a del of the entity a field points to leaves that field null
cases.why: spec 13 §5: every reference to a deleted entity goes, and where it was the only value it reads as null, as a deleted root does - not an empty object, and not a dangling reference

cases.name: at and list for a result the client does not hold are ignored, and the rest of the patch still applies
cases.why: spec 13 §3: the patch frame names a result this client never asked for - the same operation with other arguments - so its result-scoped operations are ignored rather than an error, and applied to no other result. The set acts on the cache as a whole and still lands, because every operation is total
